extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in theatre history and censorship of American plays
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic entry summarizing the 1921 Broadway play The Demi-Virgin: plot, production, cast, legal controversies over obscenity, critical reception, box-office performance, and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: New York penal law obscenity prohibition (section 1140a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused of violating section 1140a of the New York state penal law, which prohibited involvement in "any obscene, indecent, immoral or impure drama, play, exhibition, show or entertainment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory standard used to bring criminal charges against producers for alleged obscene theatrical productions; it frames legal evaluative criteria for whether a play may be subject to prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrate McAdoo's obscenity finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrate William McAdoo ruled the play was obscene, describing it as "coarsely indecent, flagrantly and suggestively immoral, impure in word and action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial language exemplifies the moral/decency threshold applied by local courts at the time — emphasis on coarse indecency, suggestive immorality, and impurity of words/actions (e.g., suggestive dialogue, stripping scene, revealing costumes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local official censorship / licensing standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The city's Commissioner of Licenses found the play "indecent and subversive of public morals" and attempted to revoke the theater's operating license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative/municipal authorities evaluated productions against public morals standards and could seek license revocation; the appeals court later limited that administrative power (ruled commissioner lacked authority to revoke once license granted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based objections used by critics and censors
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary reviewers and censors condemned the play as immoral due to its sexual situations and suggestive dialogue; attention was drawn to female cast wearing revealing gowns/bedroom attire and the "Stripping Cupid" scene where actresses removed clothing onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluative factors for perceived indecency included sexual situations, suggestive lines, explicit striptease-like staging, and revealing costuming; critics invoked these when calling for censorship or condemning the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic/critical criteria (humor, plotting, novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reviewers panned the play as "unfunny and vulgar," called it "trash," criticized weak plotting and overreliance on lewd dialogue and stripping instead of better plotting and humor, while a minority found it entertaining or not as shocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical assessment used conventional artistic criteria — comic effectiveness, plot quality, originality/novelty, and wit — alongside moral judgments; negative reviews cited poor plotting, stale genre, and lack of genuine humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as an evaluative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite negative reviews and legal troubles, the play was one of the most successful of the 1921–22 season, with high weekly box office receipts ($12,000 rising to $14–17,000) and over 200,000 tickets sold across 268 performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box-office performance, ticket sales, touring productions, and marketing exploitation of controversy were treated as measures of a play's success or cultural impact independent of critical approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standards for adjudication (grand jury / jury trial pathway)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the magistrate's ruling, Woods requested transfer of the case to the Court of General Sessions (which provided jury trials and required indictment by grand jury); the grand jury dismissed the case the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal procedure — whether a matter proceeds to a grand jury, availability of jury trial — affected whether obscenity allegations resulted in indictment/conviction; prosecutorial burden and procedural posture influenced outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-context / temporal standards of decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that what was scandalous in 1921 could be suppressed pre–World War I, while a decade later bedroom-farce sexual attitudes would be seen as unsophisticated; changing cultural norms affected judgments about decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of obscenity or offensiveness depend on prevailing social mores and historical context; producers and censors assessed material relative to contemporary standards rather than an absolute metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producer strategies affecting reception (publicity via controversy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producer A. H. Woods exploited controversy and legal proceedings to boost ticket sales, advertising the show's notoriety and reporting attendance figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotional choices and the use of controversy can alter public perception and commercial outcomes; this is an implicit criterion for producing and marketing theatrical works.
